body.title: Sacred Earth and River Silt: Kumartuli Clay to Gangetic Immersion
body.summary: Tracing the philosophical and ecological continuum of ephemeral clay ritual from Hooghly silt to Gangetic Visarjan.

rationale.text: Both traditions celebrate transience: divinity is given tangible form in clay harvested from the sacred river, worshipped with seasonal ecstasy, and surrendered back into the flowing water without permanent monuments.

whyItMatters.text: This philosophy of deliberate transience contrasts with Western monumental permanence, offering a profound indigenous ecological framework for art and worship.

body.doesNotEstablish: This relationship does not suggest that idol sculpting in Bengal and cremation rituals in Varanasi follow identical liturgical manuals, but reveals a shared philosophical worldview concerning elemental return.
body.uncertainty: Local theological interpretations of clay dissolution differ between regional Tantric and Puranic traditions.

claims.text: Indian river traditions emphasize that clay forms are temporary vessels for eternal spiritual principles.

evidence.excerpt: The immersion reinforces the philosophical notion that all forms return to their primordial elemental state.

claims.text: Traditional clay sculpting was designed to leave no trace, dissolving harmlessly into the river ecosystem.

evidence.excerpt: Unbaked clay and vegetable colors historically ensured natural ecological degradation in the river.
